sections.title: Purpose
sections.summary: States the manual's purpose: guidance for designing reinforced concrete hydraulic structures (RCHS) by the strength design method. Plain concrete and prestressed concrete are explicitly out of scope.
sections.body: This engineer manual provides guidance for designing reinforced concrete hydraulic structures by the strength design method. Plain concrete and prestressed concrete are not covered in this manual.
key_points: Covers strength design of reinforced concrete hydraulic structures (RCHS) only
Plain concrete and prestressed concrete are explicitly excluded

sections.title: Discussion
sections.summary: Frames the manual as covering RCHS strength-design requirements for both serviceability and ultimate strength, adopting industry standards as applicable, with a nod to USACE Environmental Operating Principles.
sections.body: This manual covers requirements for design of reinforced concrete hydraulic structures (RCHS) by the strength design method. It is applicable to all hydraulic structures and contains provisions for design of structures satisfactory for both serviceability and ultimate strength. Industry design and construction standards have been adopted as applicable. Users are also responsible for incorporating the USACE Environmental Operating Principles wherever possible.
key_points: Applicable to all hydraulic structures
Covers both serviceability and ultimate strength design
Industry standards (ACI, AASHTO, ASCE, ASTM) adopted as applicable

sections.title: Background
sections.summary: Explains why RCHS need manual-specific guidance beyond plain ACI 318-19: severe exposure (submergence, wave action, spray, icing, chemical attack), typical RCHS types (stilling basins, floodwalls, lock/dam structures, intake/outlet towers), the need for low permeability and crack control over a 100-year design service life, and load factors modified from ACI 318-19 to reflect hydraulic-structure-specific loads and higher required reliability for critical structures. Notes RCHS are typically lightly reinforced (rho < 1 percent) with limited ductility compared to building structures (rho >= 1 percent).
sections.body: Industry design and construction standards (ACI, AASHTO, etc.) are adopted as applicable to provide safe, reliable, cost-effective hydraulic structures for civil works projects. RCHS are directly subjected to submergence, wave action, spray, icing, or other severe climatic conditions, and sometimes a chemically contaminated atmosphere. Typical RCHS are stilling basin slabs and walls; concrete-lined channels; submerged features of powerhouses and pump stations; spillway piers; spray and training walls; floodwalls; submerged features of intake and outlet structures (towers, conduits, culverts); locks and dams; guide and guard walls; submerged retaining walls; and other structures for flood barriers, conveying/storing water, hydropower, water-borne transportation, and ecosystem restoration. Satisfactory long-term service requires saturated concrete highly resistant to weather-cycle and tidal-fluctuation deterioration; RCHS members must have adequate density and impermeability and sustain minimal cracking for leakage and corrosion control. Most RCHS are lightly reinforced (reinforcement ratios < 1 percent) with limited ductility compared to fully ductile reinforced concrete buildings (ratios typically >= 1 percent). Load factors resemble ACI 318-19 but are modified for unique hydraulic loads, RCHS serviceability needs, and higher reliability for critical structures. RCHS have a 100-year design service life, the basis for this manual's requirements.
key_points: RCHS face severe exposure: submergence, wave action, spray, icing, chemical attack
Typical RCHS: stilling basins, floodwalls, lock/dam structures, intake/outlet towers, conduits
Most RCHS are lightly reinforced (rho < 1%) with limited ductility vs. buildings (rho >= 1%)
100-year design service life is the basis for this manual's requirements
Load factors resemble but are modified from ACI 318-19 for hydraulic-specific loads and reliability
sections.applicability: Understanding why RCHS load factors and detailing differ from ordinary ACI 318-19 building design.

sections.title: General requirements
sections.summary: RCHS are designed by ACI 318-19 strength design except as modified herein; three performance levels (usual/unusual/extreme loads) satisfy stability, strength, and stiffness requirements (Chapter 3). Discusses glass fiber reinforced polymer (GFRP) bars: emerging but anisotropic, lower shear/compressive strength than steel, non-ductile (no yield), lower modulus, subject to creep -- not investigated for RCHS use and must not be used without a CECW-EC-approved study.
sections.body: Reference: RCHS are designed with the strength design method according to ACI 318-19, except as specified in this manual; notation matches ACI 318-19 except as defined herein. Performance: three levels of performance for stability, strength, and stiffness satisfy structural/operational requirements across usual, unusual, and extreme load categories (Chapter 3). Glass fiber reinforced polymer (GFRP) bars are emerging as a noncorrosive alternative to steel, but are anisotropic (high tensile strength only along the fiber direction), have lower shear and compressive strength than steel, do not yield (elastic until failure, nonductile), have lower modulus, and are subject to creep. GFRP has not been investigated for RCHS use and must not be used unless a strength/serviceability/deflection study is performed with CECW-EC consultation and approval, specific to the intended application.
key_points: RCHS designed per ACI 318-19 strength design except as modified herein
Three performance levels (usual/unusual/extreme) per Chapter 3
GFRP bars: anisotropic, non-ductile (no yield), lower modulus, subject to creep
GFRP prohibited for RCHS without a CECW-EC-approved study
sections.applicability: Baseline design-method statement and the GFRP-bar restriction.

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Outlines the manual's structure: Chapter 2 detailing, Chapter 3 strength/serviceability requirements (loads, load factors, reinforcement limits), Chapter 4 flexure/axial design equations (incl. biaxial bending), Chapter 5 shear design, and Appendices A-G plus a Glossary.
sections.body: This manual provides design procedures with worked examples, and derivations of the combined flexural and axial load equations. Chapter 2 presents general detailing requirements. Chapter 3 gives strength and serviceability requirements, including load factors and flexural reinforcement limits. Chapter 4 includes design equations for members subjected to flexural and/or axial loads (including biaxial bending). Chapter 5 presents shear design guidance, including curved and special straight members. Appendices: A References; B Design Equations for Flexural and Axial Loads; C Investigation Examples; D Design Examples; E Load Combinations for Design of Typical RCHS; F Commentary on Chapter 3; G Commentary on Chapter 5; plus a Glossary of Terms (acronyms, notation, unit conversion factors).
key_points: Ch 2: detailing; Ch 3: strength/serviceability/loads; Ch 4: flexure+axial (incl. biaxial); Ch 5: shear
Appendix B derives the design equations; C and D are worked examples (investigation vs. design)
Appendix E gives example load combinations by structure type; F/G are commentary

sections.title: Mandatory requirements
sections.summary: RCHS must be designed according to this manual; GFRP use requires a CECW-EC-approved strength/serviceability/deflection study.
sections.body: RCHS must be designed according to this manual. GFRP must not be used for RCHS unless a study of strength, serviceability, and deflection is performed with consultation and approval by CECW-EC.
key_points: This manual's provisions are mandatory for RCHS design
GFRP requires a CECW-EC-approved study before use
